newsitem.title: UK: PPI data show UK inflation pressures still subdued.
newsitem.headline: PPI data show UK inflation pressures still subdued.

text.p: Benign UK August producer price data show short-term inflationary pressures remain subdued but the figures are unlikely to tip the balance towards another interest rate cut, economists said.

Flat output prices and falling year-on-year input prices augur well for Thursday's August retail price numbers, but the inflation picture is nevertheless likely to deteriorate as the economy gathers steam in the months ahead.
"These are good numbers but not enough on their own to prompt a rate cut just yet," said Ian Shepherdson of HSBC.

The headline PPI numbers were in line with market expectations, with output prices unchanged month-on-month in August and up 2.0 percent year-on-year, while input prices were up 0.3 percent month-on-month and down 2.2 percent year-on-year.
Shepherdson said the key figure was output prices excluding food, drink, tobacco and petrol, which grew at an annual rate of 1.2 percent in August.

This correlates closely with a lag of a few months with the "other goods" sector, which comprises 26.2 percent of the RPI index, he said. "It suggests that a huge fall is imminent, pulling RPIX within the target range over the next few months."
The consensus forecast for August RPIX -- retail prices excluding mortgage interest payments -- is 2.7 percent year-on-year. The government target is 2.5 percent.

David Coleman of CIBC Wood Gundy said price pressures in UK manufacturing were clearly at a very low level and the PPI numbers were further justification for the June cut in official interest rates to 5.75 percent.
"Indeed, if the annualised rate for underlying output prices is used as a yardstick, inflation has fallen to almost zero in the latest three months," he said.

Coleman said the figures could strengthen Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's hand in pushing for a fifth successive rate cut at his September 23 monetary meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George, but this would be seen as a political move.
"Clarke is more likely to be influenced by the view that another easing could push his luck just a little too far."
Mark Hale of Sakura Finance said the inflation outlook remains relatively good in the near term, with good input price data and little pressure from wage costs.
But he added: "I think we will begin to see the retail price environment deteriorate slightly in the future."
"We see higher global growth, including higher commodity prices specifically, also feeding through and helping to push up UK prices in the future," Hale told Reuters Financial Television.
This meant Clarke was unlikely to be able to cut rates again wiuthout risking a negative reaction from sterling and a further steepening of the yield curve.

Chris Tinker said rising consumer spending would give hard-pressed retailers an opportunity to try to restore profit margins. "That will feed through into headline prices as we go through the turn of the year and into next year's figures."

Tinker told RFTV a further interest rate cut at this stage would bring few benefits in terms of boosting an already recovering housing market and would risk an adverse market reaction, so the Chancellor's attention was likely to shift to fiscal policy.
